title: Anointed, Betrayed, Arrested, Condemned, Denied
summary: Two days before Passover the chief priests plot Jesus' death, a woman anoints him at Bethany, and Judas agrees to betray him. Jesus eats the Passover with the Twelve, gives them bread and cup as his body and his blood of the covenant, and predicts their desertion. In Gethsemane he prays in anguish while his disciples sleep, and Judas arrives with an armed crowd. Tried at night before the high priest and council, Jesus declares that he is the Christ and is condemned, while in the courtyard Peter denies him three times.
story: The whole Gospel has been moving toward this night. Jesus predicted three times that he would be handed over, condemned, and killed; now it happens, step by step, and the Greek verb for handing over or betraying runs through the chapter. The chapter also brings the disciples' story to its lowest point. The Twelve who were called to be with him (3:14) sleep while he prays, flee when he is arrested, and their leader swears he does not know him. Yet Jesus has already promised, in verse 28, that after he is raised he will go ahead of them into Galilee, a promise the angel will repeat at the empty tomb in 16:7.
historical:
Passover commemorated Israel's deliverance from Egypt, and the Feast of Unleavened Bread followed it for seven days. Jerusalem's population swelled with pilgrims, which is why the authorities feared a riot and wanted to arrest Jesus quietly. The lambs were sacrificed in the temple on the afternoon of the 14th of the month Nisan and eaten that night, which by Jewish reckoning was the beginning of the 15th. The high priest, whom Mark does not name, was Caiaphas, who held office from about AD 18 to 36; Matthew and John name him. The Sanhedrin was the supreme Jewish council in Jerusalem, made up of chief priests, elders, and scribes, with authority over religious matters but, under Roman rule, not the right to carry out executions on its own authority.

The Mishnah, compiled around AD 200, sets rules for capital trials that forbid holding them at night or on the eve of a festival, and some readers have argued that Jesus' trial broke these rules. Others note that the Mishnah may describe later or idealized practice rather than what a priestly court did in the 30s. Mark himself presents the proceedings as a hurried hearing whose verdict was settled before it began (14:1, 14:55).
cultural:
Guests at a formal meal reclined on couches, leaning on the left elbow. Pouring perfumed oil on a guest's head was an act of honor, and pure nard was an imported aromatic oil from the Himalayan region, extremely costly; three hundred denarii was about a year's wages for a laborer. Alabaster jars had long narrow necks that might be broken to pour out the contents. A man carrying a water jar would stand out, since fetching water was usually women's work.

The Passover meal followed a pattern that later Jewish sources describe in detail: blessings over several cups of wine, unleavened bread, bitter herbs, the lamb, and the retelling of the exodus, with the singing of the Hallel psalms (Psalms 113 to 118), which is probably the hymn of verse 26. Gethsemane means oil press, and it was an olive grove on the Mount of Olives. Abba is the Aramaic word a child used for father, familiar and warm, though also used by adults. A kiss was a customary greeting between a disciple and his teacher. Tearing one's clothes was a sign of grief or horror, required of a judge who heard blasphemy. Peter's Galilean origin was evident in his speech, as Matthew's parallel says.
literary: Mark opens with another of his sandwiches: the plot of the chief priests (verses 1 and 2), the woman's anointing (3 to 9), and Judas's offer to betray (10 and 11). The unnamed woman gives lavishly; one of the Twelve sells Jesus for money. The chapter closes with a second sandwich: Peter follows into the courtyard (54), Jesus is tried inside (55 to 65), and Peter denies him outside (66 to 72). At the very moment Jesus confesses the truth before the council and is mocked as a false prophet, his prophecy about Peter is being fulfilled word for word. The story of the young man who flees naked (51 and 52) appears only in Mark and has puzzled readers; some think it is the author's own signature, others see an echo of Amos 2:16, where even the bravest flee naked on the day of judgment, but the text does not say. The whole chapter is punctuated by fulfilled Scripture and fulfilled prediction.

outline.t: Jesus predicts the disciples' desertion and Peter's denial
Jesus before the high priest and the council

doctrines.note: Jesus interprets his death at the table: his body given, his blood of the covenant poured out for many. The words echo Exodus 24:8, where Moses sealed the covenant with sacrificial blood, and Isaiah 53, where the servant bears the sin of many. His death is the sacrifice that establishes a new relationship between God and his people.

The Lord's Supper is instituted here. Christians agree that Jesus commanded it and that it proclaims his death, but they differ on how Christ is present in it: Roman Catholic and Orthodox churches confess a real change in the elements, Lutherans a real presence in, with, and under them, the Reformed a real spiritual presence received by faith, and many Baptists and others a memorial. These are second-order differences among churches that confess the same Lord.

Gethsemane shows prayer at its most honest: Jesus asks for the cup to pass and submits to the Father's will. It also shows the disciples' failure to pray, and Jesus' warning that the spirit is willing but the body is weak.

Before the high priest Jesus openly confesses that he is the Christ, the Son of the Blessed One, and adds that they will see the Son of Man at the right hand of Power, joining Psalm 110:1 and Daniel 7:13. The secret kept through the Gospel is now spoken plainly, and it is the confession for which he is condemned.

words.note: Diatheke, covenant, the word the Greek Old Testament uses for God's binding agreements with Noah, Abraham, Israel at Sinai, and David. Jesus speaks of my blood of the covenant, recalling Sinai, and Jeremiah 31:31 had promised a new covenant in which God would forgive sin and write his law on hearts. The cup announces that this covenant is being made.

Abba, the Aramaic for father, preserved by Mark along with its translation. It is the address of intimacy and trust, and it appears on Jesus' lips at the point of greatest anguish. Paul later says the Spirit enables believers to cry Abba, Father (Romans 8:15, Galatians 4:6), sharing the Son's own way of addressing God.

Paradidomi, to hand over or deliver, used for Judas's betrayal, for the council handing Jesus to Pilate, and in the passion predictions. The same verb can also describe God giving up his Son (Romans 8:32). Behind the human betrayals Mark lets readers see a divine purpose: the Son of Man goes as it is written of him.

Poterion, cup. Jesus gives the disciples the cup of the covenant and, hours later, asks the Father to take this cup from him. In the prophets the cup is often the cup of God's wrath (Isaiah 51:17, Jeremiah 25:15). Jesus drinks the cup of judgment so that his followers can drink the cup of blessing.

christ: This chapter shows Jesus as the Passover lamb, the covenant sacrifice, the struck shepherd, and the Son of Man. He knows what is coming and goes toward it freely: he arranges the meal, predicts the betrayal and denial, and rises from prayer to meet his betrayer. In Gethsemane his full humanity is on display; he is deeply troubled and asks that the cup pass. In the trial his full identity is declared; he is the Christ and will be seen at God's right hand. The woman's anointing, which he interprets as preparation for burial, marks him as the anointed one whose kingship will be enthroned on a cross. The church has always found in this night both the depth of Christ's suffering for sinners and the depth of his faithfulness to the Father's will.

hard.q: Was the Last Supper a Passover meal? John seems to place Jesus' death on the day the Passover lambs were killed.
hard.a: Mark, Matthew, and Luke clearly present the Last Supper as a Passover meal, eaten on the evening after the lambs were sacrificed (14:12). John's Gospel, however, says that on the morning of Jesus' trial the authorities had not yet eaten the Passover (John 18:28), and it places his death on the day of Preparation, when the lambs were slaughtered (John 19:14). Several explanations have been offered. Some think different groups in Jerusalem followed different calendars; the Qumran community, for instance, used a solar calendar, and some have suggested Jesus followed a calendar that placed Passover earlier. Others argue that John's phrases refer not to the Passover meal itself but to the week-long festival and its sacrifices, so that John and the Synoptics describe the same timeline. Still others think John has arranged his account theologically to present Jesus as the Passover lamb, or that the Synoptics have made a pre-Passover meal into a Passover. No solution commands full agreement. All four Gospels agree that Jesus died at Passover, on a Friday, and that his death was understood in light of the Passover's deliverance.

questions: The woman gave something costly and was criticized for wasting it. What would it look like for you to give Jesus something that others might think too much?
Jesus prayed, “Yet not what I will, but what You will.” Where are you being asked to pray that prayer now?
Peter's failure is told in full, and he is not written off. How does his story shape the way you think about your own failures and the failures of others?
